title: A visitor and a flower
scenario: A bee gains nectar and, in this example, pollinates the flower, improving the plant's reproduction.
why: Both partners benefit in the stated interaction, an example of mutualism. Actual costs and benefits can depend on the species and context.

title: An exchange underground
scenario: In this mycorrhizal association, the fungus receives plant carbon while the plant obtains mineral nutrients through the fungus.
why: Both partners receive benefits in the stated exchange, a mutualistic interaction. Mycorrhizal relationships vary across conditions.

title: Bacteria in a root nodule
scenario: In this root-nodule association, bacteria obtain plant resources and provide fixed nitrogen to the legume.
why: Both partners benefit in the specified association, an example of mutualism. The details of nitrogen transfer are simplified.

title: A cleaning visit
scenario: A cleaner fish obtains food by removing parasites, and in this example the host fish benefits from parasite removal.
why: Both fish benefit in this stipulated interaction, so it is mutualistic. Actual interactions can vary among species and situations.

title: A blood-feeding visitor
scenario: A tick feeds on a host's blood and benefits while harming that host.
why: The tick benefits and the host is harmed, a parasitic interaction. This sign convention describes the stated pair, not all effects on the ecosystem.

title: A gut resident
scenario: A tapeworm obtains nutrients from a host and, in this example, harms the host.
why: The parasite benefits while the host is harmed. That pattern is parasitism in the stated model.

title: A hunter and its prey
scenario: A wolf eats a deer, gaining food while the individual deer is killed.
why: The predator gains food and the individual prey is harmed, a predation interaction. Population-level effects can be more complex.

title: A leaf becomes food
scenario: A caterpillar eats a leaf, gaining food while the plant loses tissue and is harmed in this example.
why: The herbivore benefits and the plant is harmed in the stipulated case. Herbivory is a form of consumption with effects that depend on context.

title: Two seedlings share a resource
scenario: Two seedlings compete for a limiting resource, and each grows less than it would alone in this model.
why: Both have a cost relative to growing alone, so the model represents competition. Different environments can change competitive effects.

title: A scarce nesting site
scenario: Two birds compete for scarce nesting sites, reducing each bird's expected success compared with having the site uncontested.
why: Both competitors experience a cost relative to the stated uncontested baseline. The interaction is competition.

title: A nest in a tree
scenario: A bird gains a nesting site in a tree; assume the tree has no appreciable benefit or harm in this example.
why: The bird benefits and the tree is assumed unaffected, so the stipulated relationship is commensalism. Real effects should be measured rather than assumed.

title: Following a larger swimmer
scenario: A pilot fish gains food scraps near a shark; assume the shark has no appreciable benefit or harm in this example.
why: The fish benefits and the shark is assumed unaffected, making this stipulated case commensalism. Effects can differ in other situations.
